text: Size each part’s sacrificial base for its observed adhesion. Increase the footprint of a part that detaches during printing.

Keep the holder attached throughout printing and make the ties easy to remove at the hinge and battery entrance without heavy twisting or stressing the lips. Make the connectors a little thinner where they attach to the sacrificial base plate so that end also breaks away easily.

Make base and support connections easy to identify and remove without snapping useful features, leaving unwanted protruding stubs, or leaving material in functional holes, hinge seats and wire routes.
Use large adhesion bases on all parts, including tiny loose fittings.
For ordinary iteration plates, print changed or explicitly requested parts. Include requested keepers and fittings even when their geometry is unchanged.
Keep the tall or heavy holder on a broad, well-attached disposable base. Scale each small loose fitting’s own pad to its mass and orientation so it is easy to handle and remove.
R63 printed to completion. Its base grip still took substantial twisting to free at the battery entrance.
Provide access to remove support material on both sides of the key carrier without breaking permanent plastic.
If a disposable monitoring pipe or tower is included, fasten it firmly to its base through the print. Its base can remain permanently attached to the disposable piece.
Leave loose flat battery spacers off routine plates. Include them for a particular fit trial and reprint a matching door when its interface changes.

On the printed R69, freeing the carrier near the battery slot required force and tore a small hole from useful material. Improve that local sacrificial connection while preserving proven overall bed adhesion.

After removing the printed R70, the user reported that the base connectors were still hard to rip from the base plate and little bits protruded after removal. Exact affected connectors and residual stub sizes were not measured.
